historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Direct factor Xa inhibitors

starting.description: There was no single documented start for every program. Natural inhibitors, including antistasin, showed factor Xa inhibition and anticoagulant activity; discoverers describe natural-inhibitor studies as preceding the later focus on small-molecule inhibitors. Rivaroxaban arose from a targeted screen with active synthetic hits. Separately, a recognized biological sequence similarity prompted the apixaban team's screening of a platelet-inhibitor library; active isoxazolines became its leads. In the Daiichi branch, a working synthetic inhibitor, DX-9065a, prompted later non-amidine research, although the original clue for that earlier program remains unestablished.

inspiration.description: Natural-factor studies supplied target-feasibility evidence; recognition of factor Xa's biological substrate relationship helped motivate one library screen. Observed activities of synthetic screening hits and of the DX-9065a prototype provided later starting points for medicinal-chemistry programs. These are distinct links, not a claim that all oral inhibitors derive structurally from antistasin.

steps.description: In 1987 antistasin, purified from a leech salivary gland extract in antimetastatic research, was observed to inhibit factor Xa and coagulation; the authors hypothesized an Xa-mediated anticoagulant mechanism.

Discoverer retrospectives describe natural-inhibitor studies as evidence for the target and a subsequent focus on small-molecule direct inhibitors; they do not claim a shared natural chemical scaffold.
In the rivaroxaban branch, factor Xa assays of a chemical collection yielded active hits, which were optimized into the candidate.

In the apixaban branch, recognized sequence similarity motivated screening of an antiplatelet library; active isoxazolines underwent modeling and multiple structural revisions into the bicyclic oral candidate.

In a separate Daiichi program, reported to have started in 1979, the active but poorly orally absorbed DX-9065a prototype preceded structure–activity research and screening of non-amidine compounds; this led to the later oral candidate DU-176b, edoxaban.

design.description: Researchers deliberately screened and redesigned active compounds for inhibition, selectivity, antithrombotic activity and oral availability. In the apixaban branch, structure-based redesign changed the lead architecture into a bicyclic candidate; in the Daiichi branch, replacing basic amidine groups and screening non-amidine compounds led to an oral candidate with measured changes in potency and selectivity as well as absorption.

circumstances.description: The specific events classified as planned are the factor Xa-directed chemical screens and subsequent optimization, including the apixaban library screen and Daiichi non-amidine research; this is not a claim that every earlier observation was anticipated.

limits: The documented class-level judgment rests on natural-factor studies and on observation-led development of active synthetic hits or prototypes; it does not establish that every company began from the same observation.

Daiichi's reported 1979 program start predates the 1987 antistasin report. The source evidence does not establish that antistasin initiated that program or was the chemical scaffold for any cohort drug.

The observed DX-9065a prototype supports the later Daiichi development sequence, while the founding 1979 clue and earliest chemical lead remain unestablished. The 2011 rivaroxaban historical account was read in abstract only; contemporaneous initial screening papers were not read.
conflicts: S4 calls DX-9065a the first direct factor Xa inhibitor without qualification, whereas S3 reports factor Xa inhibition by the natural protein antistasin in 1987; the intended scope of the priority claim is not explicit.

S4 dates the Daiichi program to 1979; a publisher-indexed snippet from a 2009 Daiichi research paper appears to date an investigation to 1981, but the full text could not be opened and the potentially different project boundaries were not verified. See receipt.
gaps: The initiating clue and first chemical lead of Daiichi's program are not reported in S4 or S5; the evidence links DX-9065a to later non-amidine development but not every intermediate chemical step.

The original apixaban and rivaroxaban lead-screening reports and the 2009 article's full text were not read; the possible 1979-versus-1981 discrepancy remains unresolved. S6 was read in abstract only.
